For this one, who offers the peace offerings, is without doubt already conscious of his own salvation; and therefore he who has arrived at salvation must of necessity offer things that are great and perfect. For thus the Apostle too says: "solid food, however, is for the perfect".

"But if this house be a priest's", he says, "or a Levite's, wherever it be, whether in a city or in a field, it always has redemption". In this place I seek the priestly sense and the Levitical understanding. For the hearer of these things ought not, if it can be, to be inferior to that very one who wrote and sanctioned these things. What is it, then, that the priest and the Levite "always" and wherever it be "has redemption" of his house? According to the spiritual understanding a priest is called a mind consecrated to God, and he is named a Levite who unceasingly stands beside God and ministers to his will. Perfection, therefore, in understanding and work, in faith and deeds, is to be taken as the priest and the Levite. And so, if it should ever happen to this perfect mind to sell the "house which it has not made with hands, eternal in the heavens", and to give it into the hands of…

But concerning these things, so far as we were able, we have explained in the foregoing; now, however, we add this, that it says: "in the place in which the whole burnt offerings are slaughtered, there also the victims for sin". See how great is the mercy and kindness of God, that where the "whole burnt offering" is slaughtered — that which is offered to God alone — there also the "victim" which is "for sin" is commanded to be immolated; so that, namely, he who has sinned and repents, "being turned to God", and slays the victim of "a contrite spirit", may understand that he now stands in a "holy place" and is joined to those things which pertain to God. There, then, is the "victim for sin" immolated, where also the "whole burnt offering": "in the sight," it says, "of the Lord". It is perhaps possible to offer a sacrifice "in the sight of the Lord" and to offer not "in the sight of the…

After this: "this is," it says, "the law of the sacrifice which the sons of Aaron the priest shall offer before the altar in the presence of the Lord. He shall take from it a full hand of the fine flour of the sacrifice with its oil and with all its frankincense, which are for the sacrifice, and shall place upon the altar the victim, an odor of sweetness, its memorial to the Lord. But what remains of it, Aaron and his sons shall eat. Unleavened it shall be eaten in a holy place; in the court of the tabernacle of testimony they shall eat it. It shall not be cooked leavened; this portion I have given to them from the offerings of the Lord; they are a holy of holies, as is that for sin and for offense. All the males of the priests shall eat it; a perpetual statute throughout your generations, from the offerings of the Lord. Everyone who touches these things shall be sanctified." In these…

Therefore the sacrifice, for which all these sacrifices had gone before in type and figure, one and perfect — "Christ" has been "immolated." If anyone "touches" the flesh of this sacrifice, he is immediately "sanctified"; if he is unclean, he is healed, if he is under a "plague." Thus at last did she understand — she of whom I made mention a little before, "who was suffering an issue of blood" — that he himself was the flesh of the sacrifice and the flesh of the "holy of holies"; and because she truly understood what was the flesh of the "holy of holies," for this reason she drew near. And indeed she does not dare to touch the holy flesh itself — for she had not yet been cleansed, nor had she grasped the things that are perfect — but she "touched the fringe of the garment" with which the holy flesh was covered, and by her faithful touch she drew forth "power" from the flesh which both…

But the offerings of the soul it describes as far inferior. This soul has neither a "bull-calf" nor a "sheep" nor a "kid" to offer to God; but it does not even find "a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons". It has only "fine flour"; from it, it "offers unleavened loaves from the oven", from it a work made "in the pan" or "mixed with oil on the griddle". Whence it seems to me that the one here called "a soul" is to be understood as that man whom Paul names "the animal (natural) man"; who, even if he is not pressed by sins nor headlong toward vices, nevertheless does not have anything spiritual in him, anything that might figuratively be reckoned the flesh of the Word of God. For thus Paul the Apostle himself says of him that: "the animal (natural) man does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God. For it is foolishness to him, and he cannot understand, because it is…

But if you wish to incline these things also to the moral level, you too have a "calf" which you ought to offer. Your flesh is a "calf," and indeed a very proud one; and if you wish to offer it as an offering to the Lord, so as to keep it chaste and modest, lead it "to the door of the tabernacle," that is, where it may be able to receive the hearing of the divine books. Let your offering be "male," let it not know woman, let it spurn concupiscence, let it flee frailty, let it seek nothing dissolute or soft. "Lay" also "your hand upon" your "victim," that it may be acceptable to the Lord, and slaughter it "before the Lord," that is, place upon it the bridle of continence, and do not take away from it the hand of discipline, just as that man laid his hand upon his own flesh who said: "I macerate my body and subject it to servitude, lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself…

But now let us see what is written also in what follows concerning the shewbread. "And you shall take", it says, "fine flour and make from it twelve loaves; of two tenths shall be one loaf; and you shall set them in two rows, six loaves in one row, upon the clean table before the Lord. And you shall put upon the row clean frankincense and salt, and the loaves shall be set as a memorial before the Lord; on the day of the sabbaths they shall always be set forth before the Lord by the children of Israel, an everlasting covenant. And it shall be Aaron's and his sons', and they shall eat them in a holy place; for they are the holy of holies. This shall be theirs of the things that are offered to the Lord, an everlasting statute". According to what is written, in the twelve loaves a "memorial before the Lord" seems to be made of the twelve tribes of Israel, and a command to be given that…

But let us now see what is the making of these shewbread loaves which are commanded to be "always placed before the Lord". "Of two tenths", it says, "let there be one loaf". He said "two tenths" indeed, but of what measure these "tenths" are he did not specify; although surely it would have been consistent, if he wished the quantity of the fine flour to be known, to name the measure itself of which he commanded "two tenths" to be taken. What, then, is this thing whose measure and amount could neither be specified nor named? The number ten is everywhere found to be perfect; for from it arises the reckoning and origin of every number. Fittingly, therefore, the author and origin of all things, God, is seen to be shown under this number. But if in the church I speak of the Father alone and utter the praises of him alone, I have made a loaf of one tenth. Or if I make a discourse concerning…

Both this one, who "found perdition," and that one who found "robbery," and also he who "denied the deposit," and everyone whosoever in any part "has harmed the soul of his neighbor and has sworn unjustly": "he shall restore," it says, "the principal itself and shall add a fifth part over and above, and to him whose it is he shall render it," according, at least, to that exposition concerning the adding of the fifth parts which we have already given before. "And he shall offer," it says, "to the Lord a ram of the sheep without blemish, at a price, for that in which he offended; and the priest shall pray for him before the Lord, and it shall be remitted him for the one of all the things which he did and offended in it." We have said above what it is to offer a "ram," and this one bought "at the price of the holy shekel." Now it remains for us to state that difference — that there he…

It is said, then, in what follows: "but if it be a vow, or if he sacrifice his gift voluntarily, on whatever day he shall have offered his sacrifice, it shall be eaten, and on the following day. And what remains over of the flesh of the sacrifice until the third day shall be burned with fire. But if by eating anyone eats of the flesh on the third day, it shall not be accepted from him who offers it, it shall not be reckoned to him, it is a defilement. And whatever soul eats of it shall bear the sin". This is doubtless what David too says in the Psalms: "let his prayer become sin", when not only nothing of merit, but even much of guilt is sought from the sacrifices. For you hear the lawgiver decree that, if anyone eats of that "which has remained over to the third day, he shall bear the sin". Whence it is to be recognized how great a stain of sins threatens the human condition, since sin…

For just as flesh, if it be not sprinkled with salt, however great and choice it be, is corrupted, so also the soul, unless it be in some way salted with continual temptations, immediately is dissolved and grows slack. Whence it is clear that on this account it was said that "every sacrifice shall be salted with salt."

"And any flesh that has been touched by anything unclean shall not be eaten, it shall be burned with fire. Everyone who is clean shall eat the flesh; and whatever soul eats the flesh of the sacrifice of the peace offering, which is the Lord's, and his uncleanness is in him, that soul shall perish from his people. And whatever soul touches any unclean thing, whether from the uncleanness of a man or of unclean quadrupeds or from any unclean abomination, and eats of the flesh of the sacrifice of the peace offering, which is the Lord's, that soul shall perish from his people". The lawgiver here has set forth threefold causes of uncleanness. One, that the "flesh" of the sacrifices not be touched by any "uncleanness". Another, that he who eats the "flesh of the sacrifice" not be unclean and "his uncleanness be in him". The third, that, even if the flesh be clean and he who eats be himself…

After these things it follows: "and the Lord spoke," it says, "to Moses, saying: command Aaron and his sons, saying: this is the law of the whole burnt offering. This whole burnt offering shall be in its burning upon the altar all night until morning, and the fire of the altar shall burn upon it and shall not be extinguished. And the priest shall put on himself the linen tunic, and shall put on the linen undergarment about his body, and shall take away the victim which the fire has consumed, the whole burnt offering, from the altar, and shall place it beside the altar. And he shall strip himself of his robe and be clothed with another robe, and shall cast out the victim which has been burned outside the camp into a clean place. And the fire upon the altar shall burn and shall not be extinguished; and the priest shall burn wood upon it in the morning, and shall heap the whole burnt…

The discourse concerns the sacrifices which are offered by those who have sinned through ignorance or not by will. Hence also in what went before, when we were speaking of the high priest's sacrifice, we observed that it was not written of him that he had been in ignorance. But if anyone remembers well the things that were said, he can say to us that the sacrifice which we said the high priest offered "for sin" we set down as holding the figure of Christ. And it will not seem fitting that Christ, "who knew no sin", should be said to have offered a sacrifice "for sin", even though the matter is transacted through a mystery and the same one is set down both as high priest and as victim. See, therefore, whether we can meet this too in this way: that Christ indeed "did no sin", yet was made "sin for us"; while he who was in the form of God deigns to be in the form of a servant; while he who…

Let us see, then, in what order the high priest is appointed. "Moses," he says, "gathered together the congregation, and says to them: This is the word which the Lord commanded." Although, therefore, the Lord had commanded concerning the appointing of the high priest and the Lord had chosen him, nevertheless the congregation too is gathered together. For in the ordination of a priest there is required also the presence of the people, so that all may know and be assured that the one who is more excellent out of all the people, who is more learned, who is more holy, who is more eminent in every virtue, that one is chosen for the priesthood, and this with the people standing by, lest afterward any reconsideration should arise for anyone, lest any scruple should remain. This is, moreover, what the Apostle too commanded in the ordination of a priest, saying: "It is fitting also that he have…

The fifth kind of leprosy is when "a contagion is formed on the head or in the beard of a man or a woman, so that the appearance of the contagion itself is lower than the skin of the body; and this is the leprosy of the head or of the beard." See, then, whether it can happen that "leprosy of the head" be thought to be in him who has not "Christ as his head," but some other — for example, Epicurus, who preaches pleasure as the highest good; does not both the head and the beard of such a man seem to you unclean? But also he who, whereas he ought to be a man and to act as one perfect, if perchance he is easily and as a boy overcome by sin, he too must be said to have "leprosy of the beard," because, whereas he ought to overcome the evil one and to proceed with priestly honor, which is designated in the beard, hindered by the vices of adolescence, he suffers "leprosy of the beard." But that…

But let us see who this is who receives that one whose "lot has become the scapegoat's", that he may cast him "into the wilderness". "A man" it says "ready shall receive the goat which has come into his lot, upon whom the lot of the scapegoat has fallen, and shall lead him away into the wilderness." The end of this lot is the "wilderness", that is, a deserted place, deserted of virtues, deserted of God, deserted of righteousness, deserted of Christ, deserted of every good. And so upon each of us too awaits one lot of the two. For either, acting well, we are "the Lord's lot", or, acting badly, our lot leads us "to the wilderness". Do you wish that I show you evidently how those two lots are always at work and each one of us becomes either "the Lord's lot" or "the scapegoat's" or "the wilderness'"? Consider in the Gospels that "rich man" living "splendidly" and luxuriously, and "Lazarus…

But the second kind of leprosy is, if "it shall have flowered," it says, "in the skin, so that it covers all the skin of the body from the head even to the feet, throughout all things whatsoever the priest shall have inspected." When, then, it shall have covered over "all the skin of the body," then the priest pronounces him to be "clean" from the contagion. But "on whatsoever day there shall appear in him living color," again "he is judged unclean" through this, that "living color has appeared in him" which he did not have before. Concerning this some even before me have said that "living color" indicates the reason of life which is in man; and while this reason is not yet set in the soul, if any of that sin be done, it is not reckoned, for the reason that he who transgresses seems not yet capable of reason; but when reason has found place and time in him, if he now does anything…

Therefore in the shadow of this meli tree the bride longs to abide — or the Church, as we said, in the protection of the Son of God, or the soul fleeing all the remaining doctrines and clinging to the one Word of God alone, whose sweet fruit she also has in her throat, that is, by meditating unceasingly on the law of God, and by always ruminating upon it like a clean animal.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 3

quotes.quote: "Every", it says, "beast that divides the hoof, and has hooves, and brings up rumination among the cattle, these you shall eat. Besides, of these you shall not eat, which bring up rumination, and do not divide the hooves, and have hooves. The camel, because it brings up rumination, and does not divide the hoof, this is unclean to you. And the hare, because it brings up rumination, and does not divide the hoof, this is unclean to you; and the hedgehog, because it brings up rumination, and does not divide the hoof, this is unclean to you; and the swine", and so forth. It decrees, then, that animals of this kind be not eaten, which in part seem to be clean and in part unclean; as "the camel, from the fact that it ruminates", seems clean, but from the fact "that it does not have divided hooves", it is called "unclean". After these it now names also "the hare" and "the hedgehog", but says…

Scripture says, then: "the little breast of setting-apart and the arm of removal you shall eat in a holy place, you and your sons and your house with you; for it is given as a statute to you and a statute to your sons of the peace offerings of the children of Israel, the arm of removal and the little breast of setting-apart". Not every little breast is a "little breast of setting-apart", nor is every arm of "removal" or "separation" an "arm". But since we have recalled the person of the high priest to my Lord Jesus and to his sons the holy Apostles, let us see how he himself indeed eats the "little breast of setting-apart", and his sons, but the others cannot all eat the "little breast of setting-apart". What, then, is it that is set apart from all things and is not common with the rest, except the sole substance of the Trinity? If, then, I understand indeed the reckoning of the world,…

Recently there was recited in the ears of the Church the word of God saying: "Be holy, for I too am holy, the Lord your God". What this name "holy" intends for itself, and what it signifies in the divine Scriptures, must be inquired into more diligently, so that, when we have learned the force of the word, we may also be able to fulfill its work. Let us therefore gather from the divine Scriptures those things over which we find the word "holy" said, and we discover that not only human beings, but even dumb animals are called "holy"; we find also that "vessels" of the ministry are called "holy", and that vestments are said to be "holy", and no less the places which are set within cities or suburbs and assigned to the priests. Among the dumb animals indeed, the "firstborn" of oxen or of flocks are commanded by the law to be sanctified to the Lord, and it is said: do not, it says, perform…

But what is added after these things? "He shall take to wife a virgin of his own kindred, but a widow and one cast out and a harlot he shall not take, but he shall take a virgin of his own kindred; and he shall not defile his seed among his people; I am the Lord, who sanctify him". Since therefore the order of the whole exposition has been recalled to the true "great priest", Christ, let us now see also what ought to be understood about his nuptials. Paul the Apostle says: "but I wish to present you all as a chaste virgin to one husband, to Christ. But I fear lest, as the serpent seduced Eve by his craftiness, your senses be corrupted from the simplicity which is in Christ". Paul therefore wishes to "present all the Corinthians as a chaste virgin to Christ"; which assuredly he would never wish, unless he saw it to be possible. Whence perhaps it may seem wonderful how these, who came to…

"But a widow and one cast out and one defiled he shall not take". If any of us has sinned, he is "cast out"; even if he is not cast out by the bishop, whether because it lies hidden or because he is sometimes judged unto grace, he is nevertheless "cast out" by the very consciousness of sin. Nor does the grace of man avail, when Christ does not receive such a soul into marriage as "cast out". Therefore "neither a widow", as we said above, "will he take, nor one cast out nor one polluted". She is called "polluted" who, even if she has not completely committed the sin, yet by this very thing that she thought it, that she wished it, that she desired it, even if she did not carry it out, is "polluted" and is not chosen by the "great high priest". For he requires an exceedingly pure, exceedingly clean and sincere soul, which he may join to himself, because "he who is joined to the Lord is one…

These things indeed have been said generally concerning animals; but those "which are in the waters", because they are said, if indeed they have "fins and scales", to be clean, but if they do not have them, unclean and not to be eaten: this is shown in them, that, if anyone is in these waters and set in the sea of this life and in the waves of the world, he ought nevertheless to strive earnestly not to lie in the depths of the waters, as are those fishes which are said "not to have fins nor scales". For this is reported to be their nature, that they always tarry in the lowest place and about the very mud; as are eels and things like this, which cannot ascend to the surface of the water nor reach its upper parts. But those fishes which are aided by "little fins" and fortified with "scales" ascend rather to the upper parts and become nearer to this air, as those who seek the liberty of…

Something of this sort has also been written about Aaron in the book of Leviticus, namely, that "he raised up his hands over the people and blessed them." I gather from this that the saying expresses a mystery, namely, that the one who blesses someone must be adorned with works that distinguish him from the many and raise him above them. For when he is going to bless the people, the hands of Aaron are raised on high. So if someone has his hands down toward earthly things, he does not intend to bless anyone.
quotes.source_title: FRAGMENT ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 257

quotes.quote: The Apostle briefly shows the reason why these things that are read to us can be understood or not understood, saying that from his eyes "the veil of the old testament can be taken away, whoever shall have turned to the Lord"; from which he wished it to be known that, the less these things are plain to us, the less is our conversion to God. And therefore we must strive with all our strength that, being free from the occupations of the world and from worldly affairs, and leaving behind even those superfluous tales of our companions, if it can be done, we may give our effort to the word of God and "meditate on his law day and night", so that, being converted with our whole heart, we may be able to behold the unveiled and open face of Moses, and especially in these things which have now been read, whether concerning the priestly vestments or concerning the consecration of the high priest,…

We find, then, that six kinds are set forth concerning the leprosy of men, which six kinds are described in this manner. For either "in the skin of the body there comes a scar and a whitish sign in the skin of his body, the contagion of leprosy." Or "the leprosy flowering shall flower, and shall cover all the skin with the contagion from the head even to his feet." Or the third kind: "in the skin of the flesh there comes an ulcer and it is healed; and in the very place of the ulcer there comes a white scar." Or "in the skin of the flesh there comes a burning of fire, and" after these things "the healed burning shall be shining white, or bright with redness." The fifth kind, "when in a man or a woman there comes on the head or in the beard the contagion of leprosy." But the last kind is written, "when in baldness or in forehead-baldness there comes the contagion of reddish leprosy,"…

The third law concerning lepers is, "when in the skin of the body an ulcer is formed, and in the place of the ulcer a white scar with redness is found." But the cause of an ulcer is when in the body a filthy and noxious humor abounds. So then also in the soul are understood as ulcers those things which boil up from unclean desires or filthy thoughts. And if perchance these have been cured through the grace of faith and the remission of sins, and the soul has been made whole, nevertheless there remains "a scar," and that "scar" does not have a color like that of the body, but is "whiter," it is pronounced to be "leprosy." For a desire is so shining and clear that even to those who look further it shows the indications of the sin residing in it, and perhaps of such a "sin" as is "unto death"; and therefore it is described not only to be "a white scar," but also "reddish." But as to his…

But "one soul", it says, "if it should sin, shall likewise offer a female goat", according to that substitution of victims which we mentioned above. But perhaps the hearers of the church may say: it was dealt with almost better among the ancients than with us, when, sacrifices being offered by diverse rites, pardon was granted to those who sinned. Among us there is only one pardon of sins, which is given at the beginning through the grace of the laver; after this no mercy is granted to the one who sins, nor any pardon. It befits indeed a Christian, "for whom Christ died", to be of stricter discipline. For them sheep, goats, oxen were slaughtered, and birds, and fine flour was sprinkled; for you the Son of God was slaughtered, and does it delight you to sin again? And yet, lest these things lift up your spirit not so much toward virtue as cast it down toward despair, you have heard how…

But let us see what is also to be thought concerning the things that have just now been read: "but if", it says, "one soul should sin unwillingly from the people of the land, by doing one of all the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done, and should transgress, and the sin which it sinned should become known to it, it shall bring its gift: it shall bring a female goat from the kids, without blemish, for the sin which it sinned". And after this it recounted the whole rite of the sacrifice, according to what we expounded above. Concerning the soul which, made under sin, it says offers, how it is to be thought, we have explained in the foregoing as far as we could; but what it added in this place, saying "a soul, if it should sin from the people of the land", does not seem to me idle. For who would doubt that the things which the law says are said to souls or to a people that are…

"But if a ruler", it says, "should sin, he shall offer a goat from the she-goats". This ruler can be seen as the power of reason which is within us. And if this should sin in us, and we should do something foolish, that sentence of the Savior is to be greatly feared by us, which says: "you are the salt of the earth. But if the salt should lose its savor, it is good for nothing, except to be cast out and trodden underfoot by men". This one too, then, has his own victim.

We indeed, who are of the Church, rightly receive Moses and read his writings, understanding this about him: that he is a prophet, and that, by God's revealing to him, he wrote down in symbols and figures and allegorical forms the mysteries to come, which we teach to have been fulfilled in their own time. But whoever does not receive in him a meaning of this kind, whether he be one of the Jews or even one of our own, cannot show him to be a prophet at all; for how will he prove him a prophet, whose letters he asserts to be commonplace, aware of nothing future and containing no hidden mystery? And so, as this man who thinks in this way reads these things, the divine word rebukes him and says: "Do you suppose you understand what you read?" There is, then, the law, and all the things that are in the law, according to the Apostle's judgment, "imposed until the time of correction"; and just…

Ours, therefore — that is, we who do not "serve the shadow and the copy," but the truth — this is the Day of Atonement for us, on which the remission of sins has been given to us, when "Christ our Passover has been sacrificed." How then, having come to know the truth, "do we turn back again to the weak and beggarly elements of this world, to which you wish to be enslaved anew from the beginning, observing days and months and seasons and years?" Hear how the prophet too rejects a fast of this kind and says: "This is not the fast I have chosen, says the Lord, nor a day for a man to humble his soul." You, if you wish to fast according to Christ and "to humble your soul," every time of the whole year lies open to you; nay rather, have all the days of your whole life "for humbling your soul," if indeed you "have learned" from the Lord our Savior "that he is meek and humble of heart." When,…

"And the threshing shall reach for you unto the vintage". If good seed has been sown in my soul and, having received "rain" from God, it has grown and come to the ear, of necessity the harvest also will follow; and if the harvest, then also "threshing" will follow, in which the grains are cleansed. For indeed the soul which germinates from the word of God and, watered by the heavenly "rain", produces its sprout unto harvest, it is necessary that the very harvest which it brings forth be cleansed on the floor, that is, that the meanings which the soul has begotten it bring forth into the midst, and confer them—the things which it perceives—either with the other teachers or even with the divine volumes themselves; so that, if there be anything in them empty and superfluous, if there be anything like chaff or awns, it may shake it out with the spirit of discernment blowing within it, and…

But if there be a sin "of the whole synagogue", the synagogue is none the less commanded to offer "a bull-calf" as a whole burnt offering. But in the sin of the synagogue it is said: "if it should be ignorant, and the matter be hidden from the eyes of the synagogue, and it should do one of all the commandments of the Lord which shall not be done"; from which it is clear that "the whole synagogue" too can transgress through ignorance. And this the Lord also confirms in the gospels, when he says: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do".

But meanwhile she "who has borne a male," "on the eighth day" both the one who is born is circumcised and she is made clean. It is a matter of great labor for these things to happen in this brevity of time, yet, that we may say something in passing, this week may be seen as the time of the present life; for in a week of days the world was completed. In which, so long as we are set in the flesh, we cannot be pure to the point of clarity, unless the eighth day come, that is, unless the time of the age to come be present. On which day, however, he who is a male and has acted manfully is at once purified in the very coming of the age to come, and at once the mother who bore him is made clean; for she will receive the flesh purged of vices out of the resurrection. But if it had nothing virile in itself against sin, but was slack and effeminate in its acts, whose sin is such that it "is not…

Let us see, then, what it is that has now been read to us. "And the Lord spoke to Aaron, saying: You shall drink no wine nor strong drink, you and your sons with you, when you enter into the tabernacle of testimony, or when you approach the altar, and you shall not die. This is a perpetual statute throughout your generations, to distinguish between the midst of the holy and the profaned, and between the midst of the unclean and the midst of the clean, and to instruct the children of Israel in all the statutes which the Lord has spoken to them by the hand of Moses". A plain law is given both to the priests and to the chief of the priests, that "when they approach the altar, they abstain from wine and from every drink that can inebriate", which Holy Scripture is wont to name by the native word "sicera" (strong drink). The divine word wills, therefore, that the priests of the Lord be sober…

If, then, we have understood what the inebriation of the saints is, and how this is given to the saints in the promises for gladness, let us now see how our Savior does not drink wine, "until he drink it new" with the saints "in the kingdom" of God. My Savior even now mourns my sins. My Savior cannot be glad, so long as I remain in iniquity. Why can he not? Because he himself is "the advocate for our sins with the Father", as John, his fellow-initiate, declares, saying that "even if anyone has sinned, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the just; and he is himself the propitiation for our sins". How, then, can he who is "the advocate for" my "sins" drink the wine of gladness, whom I sadden by sinning? How can he who "approaches the altar" that he may make propitiation for me, a sinner, be in gladness, to whom the grief of my sins ever ascends? "With you", he says, "I will…

A narrative has been read to us whose account, though it may seem plain, will nevertheless not easily disclose to us its inner sense unless we follow rather diligently its coherence according to the letter. The passage of Scripture, then, on which we must discourse, is this: "And there went out," it says, "the son of the Israelite woman, and this one was the son of an Egyptian among the sons of Israel; and they quarreled in the camp, he who was of the Israelite woman and a man who was an Israelite. And the son of the Israelite woman, naming the name, cursed; and they brought him to Moses; and the name of his mother was Salomith, the daughter of Dabri, of the tribe of Dan. And they put him into prison, that they might judge concerning him according to the command of the Lord. And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Cast out him who cursed, outside the camp, and all who heard shall lay their…

He who is "perfect" is taught by God himself concerning the meaning of the festivals, and he does not need a man as his teacher for learning these things, but he learns from God, if anyone is able to grasp the voice of God. But he who is not such a one, but of lower rank, learns from him who has learned from God. There is, then, this twofold manner of teaching concerning the festivals. There is the one by which the prophetic mind, illumined through the Spirit, is taught — which, so to speak, is learned more by the gaze of the mind than by the sound of a voice, through which the truth itself, and not the shadow and image of the truth, is recognized. But those who cannot grasp the very brightness of God, nor behold the whole radiance of the truth with the fixed keenness of the mind, hear about the festivals in second place from those who learned first; and while the very property of…

But now let us look also at some of those things which have been read concerning clean and unclean foods or animals; and just as in the explanation of the cup we ascended from the shadow to the truth of the spiritual cup, so also concerning the foods which are spoken of through the shadow, let us ascend to those which through the spirit are the true foods. But for investigating these things we have need of the testimonies of divine Scripture, lest anyone suppose—for men love "to sharpen their tongues like a sword"—lest anyone, I say, suppose that I do violence to the divine Scriptures and drag to men the things which are related in the law concerning animals, quadrupeds or even birds or fishes, clean or unclean, and feign that these were said concerning men. For perhaps one of the hearers may say: why do you do violence to Scripture? Animals are spoken of, let animals be understood.…

But perhaps someone may say: concerning quadrupeds indeed and creeping things and birds you have rendered the reckoning, that men ought to be understood; give also concerning "those things which are in the waters". Since indeed the law designates concerning these too that some are clean and others unclean, I demand nothing in these matters, that my words be believed, unless I shall have given suitable witnesses. I will give you our very Lord and Savior Jesus Christ as witness and author of these things, how fishes are said to be men. "The kingdom of heaven is like", he says, "to a net cast into the sea, which gathers of every kind of fish; and when it has been filled, sitting upon the shore they store up those which are good in vessels; but those which are bad they cast forth". He plainly taught that those "fishes" which are said to be "gathered by the nets" are either "good" men or…

"And he girded him," he says, "according to the making of the ephod." Already above too he had said that "he girded him with the girdle" over the tunic, and now again he is girded "according to the making of the ephod". What is this double girdle, with which he wishes the high priest to be bound fast on every side? Let him be bound fast in word, bound fast in work, ready for all things, nothing slack, let him have nothing loose. Let him be girded with the virtues of the soul, let him be bound fast from bodily vices, let him fear no lapse of the soul, none of the body, let him always use both girdles, "that he may be chaste in body and spirit". And well is it that he is girded also "according to the making of the ephod". For according to his own deeds and according to his own works he will use the girdle of virtue. And after these things, he says, "he put upon him the breastpiece"—which…

"And he shall not go in to any dead soul". What is a "dead soul"? One that is dead; the prophet says: "the soul that sins, it shall die". Upon this dead soul, then, Christ does not come, because he is "wisdom", and wisdom does not enter into a malevolent soul. For that soul is dead, because in whom malice is present, sin also is present. "And sin, when it is consummated" it says "begets death". And on account of this Jesus "does not enter in to a dead soul". But if the soul lives, that is, if it has not in itself a mortal sin, then Christ, who is "life", comes to the living soul; because just as "light cannot be with darkness nor righteousness with iniquity", so neither can life be with death. And therefore if anyone is conscious to himself that he has within him a mortal sin and has not cast it from himself through the repentance of fullest satisfaction, let him not hope that Christ…

"In his father and in his mother he shall not be defiled". This passage of Scripture is most difficult to explain, but if by your prayers you entreat God the Father of the Word to deign to enlighten us, by his own gift it will be able to be explained. Everyone who enters this world is said to be brought into being in a certain defilement. On account of which Scripture also says: "no one is clean from filth, not even if his life be of one day". This very thing, then — that he is placed "in the womb" of his mother and that he takes the material of his body from the origin of the paternal seed — can be said to be "defiled in father and mother". Or do you not know that, when a male child has been made forty days old, he is offered at the altar, that he may there be purified, as one who was polluted in the very conception, whether of the paternal seed or of the maternal womb? Every man,…

After these things the Scripture adds: "and there shall not be" it says "a man, when the high priest enters within the interior veil in the tabernacle of testimony". How "shall there not be a man"? I understand it thus, that he who has been able to follow Christ and to penetrate with him the interior tabernacle and to ascend the heights of the heavens, shall now "not be a man", but according to his own word shall be "as an angel of God". Or perhaps even that word will be fulfilled concerning him which the Lord himself said: "I said, you are gods and sons of the Most High, all of you". Whether therefore, made spiritual, he becomes one spirit with the Lord, or through the glory of the resurrection passes into the order of angels, rightly he will now "not be a man"; but each one himself provides this for himself, that he either exceed the appellation of man or be reckoned within the…

The second commandment is like it, since it is the love of a human being who was made according to the image of God, and perhaps also according to his likeness. But in the exposition of the commandment which is set down concerning the love of one's neighbor, these things also must be said. For, according to what is said in the tenth Psalm, "he who loves iniquity hates his own soul", and according to what is said in Proverbs, "he who rejects discipline hates himself", it is manifest that no one who loves iniquity loves his neighbor as himself, since he does not even love himself; and no one who rejects discipline loves his neighbor as himself, seeing that he does not love his very self either. And thus it comes about that he who "loves iniquity", and "hates his own soul", cannot keep the second commandment. Likewise also "he who rejects discipline" loves some sin; and therefore he too…

After these things another law is promulgated. "Whatever soul", it says, "touches any unclean thing, or the carcass of unclean beasts, and it is hidden from him, and he is defiled; or if he touches of the uncleanness of a man, of any uncleanness by which he may be defiled", and so forth. These things indeed are observed among the Jews quite unbecomingly and uselessly. For to what end is he held unclean who has touched, for example, a dead animal or the body of a deceased man? What if it be the body of a prophet? What if the body of a patriarch, or even of Abraham himself? What if he has touched even the bones, will he be unclean? What if he touches the bones of Elisha, which raise up the dead? Will he who touches be unclean, and do the bones of the prophet make unclean even that very one whom they raise from the dead? See how unfitting the Jewish understanding is. But let us first see…

But when we wish to examine the very letter of the words as given by Matthew, "He that speaks evil of father or mother, let him die the death," consider whether it was taken from the place where it was written, "Whoso strikes his father or mother, let him die the death; and he that speaks evil of father or mother, let him die the death." For such are the exact words taken from the law with regard to the two commandments; but Matthew has quoted them in part and in an abridged form, and not in the very words.
quotes.source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 11.9

quotes.quote: Among the other sins therefore which are punished with death, the divine law reports that also "he who shall have cursed his father or mother, by death let him die". The name of father is a great mystery, and the name of mother is a hidden reverence. Your father according to the spirit is God; your mother is the "heavenly Jerusalem". Learn these things from prophetic and apostolic testimonies. This same Moses writes in the canticle: "is not this same one your father who acquired you and possessed you?". But the Apostle says concerning the "heavenly Jerusalem" that: "she is free", he says, "who is the mother of us all". First, therefore, your father is God, who begot your spirit, who also says: "I have begotten sons and exalted them". But James the Apostle also says: "let us obey the father of spirits and we shall live". Secondly, your father is the father of the flesh, by whose ministry…

Yet observe also this, that the priest himself is not said to immolate the hen; for not yet is this one, who was a leper, worthy that the priest himself immolate for him. On account of which neither is the blood of the hen offered at the altar, but it says that "the hen shall be slain in an earthen vessel, in which vessel living water has been put," so that both water may be taken up for purification and the fullness of the mystery be completed in "water and blood," which is said "to have gone out from the side" of the Savior, and no less in what John sets down in his epistle and says, that purification is made "in water and blood and spirit." Whence here too I see all these things fulfilled. For there is the "spirit" of that hen which is slain, and the "living water" which is in the vessel, and the "blood" which is poured out over it; not that we should think the grace of baptism is to…

Let us now see what law is set forth in offering victims "for sin". "And the Lord spoke", it says, "to Moses, saying: if any soul is hidden and sins unwillingly against the holy things of the Lord, he shall offer for his offense to the Lord a spotless ram of the sheep, at the price of a silver shekel of the sanctuary, for that in which he offended. And what he has sinned against the holy things, he shall restore, and shall add a fifth to it, and shall give it to the priest; and the priest shall make entreaty for him with the ram of the offense, and it shall be forgiven him". In the foregoing laws, which were reported concerning the sacrifices for uncleanness, wherever it said something was to be offered — for example, a sheep or a kid — it added: "but if his hand does not suffice for a kid or a lamb, let him offer a pair of turtledoves or two young doves", and again: "but if it does not…

Now indeed concerning the victims, some are commanded to be the high priest's own, but others are "to be taken from the people". His own is said to be the "bull-calf", which among animals is more precious and stronger; and the second animal, the "ram", which among sheep is without doubt more precious. But from the people the gifts are commanded to be offered: a "ram" from the leaders and "two goats" from the people; one that is to be sent away "into the wilderness", which is also named "the scapegoat", and one that is to be offered to the Lord. If the whole people of God were holy and all were blessed, there would not be made two lots over the goats, and one indeed bear the lot to be sent away "into the wilderness", but the other to be offered "to the Lord", but there would be one lot and one victim to the Lord alone. But now, since in the multitude of those who approach the Lord there…

But that which we say concerning the lot, let not the hearer take it as though some such lot is meant as is wont to be conducted among men by chance and not by judgment. "The Lord's lot" is to be taken as though one should say the choice of the Lord or the portion of the Lord, and again the lot of that one which is sent "into the wilderness" is to be taken as that portion which, for its own unworthiness, is spurned and cast off by the Lord. For indeed the very word "scapegoat" contains the signification of one cast off and rejected. From which we can also understand this, for example: an evil thought ascends into your heart, a desire of another man's wife or of a neighbor's possession; understand at once that this is of "the lot of the scapegoat", cast it off immediately and expel it from your heart. How do you cast it off? If you have with you the hand of the "ready man", that is, if…

Yet since the word of God is rich and, according to the judgment of Solomon, is to be "inscribed upon the heart" not simply, but doubly and "triply," let us try even now to add some things to those which were spoken a while ago according to our strength, that we may show how, "in a type of things to come," here too one goat was offered to the Lord as a victim and the other was sent away "alive." Hear in the Gospels Pilate saying to the priests and the people of the Jews: "Which of the two do you wish that I release to you, Jesus who is called Christ, or Barabbas?" Then all the people cried out that he should release "Barabbas," but hand Jesus over to death. Behold, you have the goat which was sent away "alive into the wilderness," bearing with itself the sins of the people that cried out and said: "Crucify, crucify!" This, then, is the goat sent away "alive into the wilderness," and the…

Now a third law of this kind is promulgated: "and the soul", it says, "which swears, pronouncing with its lips to do evil or to do good, according to all things whatsoever he shall utter to a man with an oath, and it is hidden from him, and afterward he knows it, and has sinned in some one of these — let him pronounce the sin which he has sinned, and he shall bring for the things in which he has offended, to the Lord, for the sin by which he has sinned, a female of the sheep" and so forth. How indeed, "if I pronounce with my lips or swear to do good" and do not do it, I am guilty of sin, there is no difficulty in showing; but how, "if I swear or pronounce to do evil" and do not do it, I have sinned, it is difficult to assign in word. For it seems absurd, for example, that if in anger I say I am going to kill a man and do not do it, I should, lest I seem to perjure myself or to deceive,…

First, concerning the "lamp" and the "lampstand" and the "oil" which is poured into it; second, concerning the "table" and the "shewbread" and their number and those who ought to use them. Let us therefore direct our mind more diligently to the things that are written, and let us pray that the grace of the Lord be granted us for discerning these things, so that in the letters which we read we may recognize what is the will of the Holy Spirit. "Command", it says, "the children of Israel, and let them bring you clean oil pressed from olives for the light, that a lamp may burn always outside the veil in the tabernacle of testimony, and Aaron and his sons shall kindle it from evening until morning before the Lord without ceasing, an everlasting statute throughout your generations. On the clean lampstand you shall kindle the lamps before the Lord until morning". He names a "clean lampstand";…

But "since the law is spiritual", let us ask of the Lord — if indeed "we have turned to the Lord" — that "the veil of the reading of the old testament be taken away" from us, so that we may be able to perceive what is the meaning of his "lampstand and lamps" according to the spiritual understanding. Before the coming of my Lord Jesus Christ the sun did not rise upon the people of Israel, but it made use of "the light of a lamp". For among them the word of the law and the prophetic word was a "lamp" shut within narrow walls, which could not pour out its light upon the whole earth. For within Judea the knowledge of God was confined, as the prophet also says: "God is known in Judea". But when the "sun of righteousness", our Lord and Savior, rose, and the man was born of whom it is written: "behold a man, the East is his name", throughout the whole world the light of the knowledge of God…

Just as "in the last days" the Word of God, clothed with flesh from Mary, came forth into this world, and one thing indeed was that which was seen in him, another that which was understood — for the appearance of the flesh in him lay open to all, but the recognition of his divinity was granted to few and to the elect —, so also, when through the prophets or the lawgiver the Word of God is brought forth to men, it is not brought forth without fitting garments. For as there it is covered by the veil of the flesh, so here by the veil of the letter, so that the letter indeed is looked upon as flesh, but the spiritual sense lying hidden within is perceived as divinity. Such, then, is what we now also find as we unroll the book of Leviticus, in which the rites of sacrifices and the diversity of victims and the ministries of the priests are described. But these things according to the letter,…

The beginning, then, of Leviticus says that "the Lord called Moses and spoke to him from the tabernacle of testimony," that he might promulgate to the sons of Israel the laws of sacrifices and of offerings, and it says: "If a man offer an offering to God, let him offer from the oxen or the flock," that is, lambs or kids; "but if from the birds, turtledoves or young of doves." "But if" not a man, but "a soul offer an offering to God, from fine flour," it says, "let him offer unleavened loaves baked in the oven, or indeed fine flour from the pan sprinkled with oil, or from the griddle likewise kneaded in oil." Then next we are taught that nothing "leavened" ought at all to be offered at the altar of God, nor should "honey" anywhere be mixed with the sacrifices, but every sacrifice or offering should be salted with "salt." In the second place he gave precept concerning the "sacrifices of…

The divine word therefore says: "and he shall place incense upon the fire in the sight of the Lord, and the smoke of the incense shall cover the propitiatory which is over the testimonies, and he shall not die. And he shall take of the blood of the bull-calf and shall sprinkle with his finger upon the propitiatory toward the east". The rite indeed of atonement for men among the ancients, which was made to God, he has taught how it should be celebrated; but you, who have come to Christ, the true high priest, who by his blood made God propitious to you and reconciled you to the Father, do not cling to the blood of the flesh; but learn rather the blood of the Word, and hear him saying to you: "this is my blood, which shall be poured out for you for the remission of sins". He who is imbued with the mysteries knows both the flesh and the blood of the Word of God. Let us not therefore linger…

But these things happen when he is indeed set within the camp, yet still "outside his own house." For it says after seven days: "on the eighth day he shall take to himself two lambs." Now not another "takes," but he himself "takes to himself." "Two lambs," it says, "without blemish, and one yearling ewe without blemish, and three tenths of fine flour sprinkled with oil, and one cyathus of oil," so that after these things, purified by a fifth purification, he may be brought to completion. Of these "two lambs," then, one indeed is immolated and is said to be "for the trespass": "in the place," it says, "in which he is slain for sin, and where the whole burnt offerings are made, in the holy place." Behold, now he is made worthy to offer sacrifice, who was able to arrive at the fifth purification, and his victim becomes "the holy of holies." But the other lamb is made "a whole burnt…

"And this is," it says, "the law of the ram which is for the trespass; the holy of holies. In the place in which they slaughter the whole burnt offerings, they shall also slaughter the ram which is for the trespass, before the Lord" and so forth. In the divine Scriptures it seems that frequently sin is named for trespass and trespass for sin indifferently and without any distinction; in this passage, however, it is found to be distinguished. For when above, in the victim "for sin", it had delivered the rite and order of the sacrifice, now it separately enjoins a sacrifice "for the trespass"; and although all things are enjoined in the same order and with the same observance, and it adds at the very end: "as that which is for sin, so also that which is for trespass; there shall be one law for them", yet it wished to show that there is some difference in those things for which it enjoined…

But let us rather quickly refer these things to ourselves, to whom the law of Christ, if we follow it, permits us to have neither possessions on earth nor houses in cities. And why do I speak of houses? It does not grant us to possess even several tunics, nor much money: for "having", he says, "food and clothing, let us be content with these". How then shall we observe the laws given concerning houses, whether set "within a walled city" or "in villages that have no walls"? We find in other places of Scripture that the divine word names a house with a certain greater mystery, as when it speaks of Jacob and sets it down as if for his praise: "for Jacob", it says, "was a simple man, dwelling in a house". And again I find it written concerning the midwives of the Hebrews: "and because", it says, "the midwives feared God, they made themselves houses". We see, then, that for the midwives the…

And similarly concerning the birds. "You shall not eat", it says, "these, because they are unclean: the eagle and the vulture", and the rest like these. For to these birds the food is always of dead bodies, and they live from dead carcasses. All, then, who lead a life of this kind must be held unclean. I think that those too are numbered among these who brood over the deaths of others and by art or fraud forge testaments. For men of this kind will deservedly be called vultures and eagles, as gaping after the carcasses of the dead. I know also other flying things which live by rapine. These are the souls which, according to this indeed—that they are rational and imbued with liberal instruction or rational disciplines—seem to be flying things; for they read and inquire either concerning the reckoning of heaven, or how the world is governed by the providence of God; according to these…

But let us too, to whom these things perhaps do not happen, see in what part the discourse of the law may build us up. And I today, though I am a sinner, yet because the dispensation of the Lord's word has been entrusted to me, seem to have the holy things of God committed to me. Nor now for the first time, but often already and long since, do we use this dispensation toward you. If, therefore, anyone of you has received from me the Lord's money and, as is wont to happen, having gone out of the church and been snatched away by the various occupations of the world, has given to oblivion the things he had heard, and has fulfilled no work from the word which he received, this is he who has not restored the money received from the holy things. Wherefore, even at hearing these things, let him call to memory that he has neglected the things which had lately been committed to him in the word…

But if perchance he shall have been made clean, he does not indeed come of his own accord and by himself to the priest, but is offered, it says, by another, nor does he enter into the camp. For neither was it fitting that "on the same day on which he was made clean," before those things which were suitable were done for him, "he should enter into the camp." On account of which "the priest," it says, "shall go out to him outside the camp." For always to him who cannot yet "enter into the camp" there "goes out" that one who can "go out outside the camp," who says: "I went out from God and came into this world." "The priest goes out," then, "to him" and considers whether he now receives health, whether he is being purged from the contagion of leprosy.

We see three distinct laws concerning the sale and redemption of houses given through Moses in Leviticus. Let us first treat their content according to the historical sense, so that afterward we may be able to ascend also to the spiritual sense. Some houses are "in walled cities", others "in villages or fields that have no walls". He says, then, that "if anyone sell a house in a walled city, let him have the opportunity of redeeming it for a full year, but after the year no power of recovering it is granted". "For it shall be", he says, "the settled possession of the buyer, if he who sold it has not been able to free it within the year". The second law is that "if the house which has been sold be in a village that has no wall, but a village to which a field lies adjacent, it shall be lawful for the seller both after the year and whenever he is able, to restore the price and recover the…

"An everlasting covenant", it says, "it shall be for Aaron and his sons, and they shall eat them in a holy place". "Aaron and his sons" are "a chosen race, a priestly race", to whom this portion of the holy things is given by God — which we all are who believe in Christ. But I do not seek the "holy place" set on earth, but in the heart. For the rational soul is called a "holy place", for which reason also the Apostle says: "do not give place to the devil". My soul, then, is the place — if I act wickedly, of the devil; if well, of God. Finally also "the evil spirit", it says, "when it has gone out from a man, and has gone about arid places, and has not found rest, then it says: I will return to my place, whence I went out". The "holy place", then, is the pure soul. In which place we are commanded to eat the food of the word of God. For it is not fitting that an unholy soul should receive…

"For they are the holy of holies". You see how he did not say holy only, but "holy of holies", as if he said: this food is not the common food of all, nor of anyone unworthy, but it belongs to "the holy". How much more shall we also say this rightly and deservedly concerning the word of God: this discourse is not for all; not just anyone can hear the mystery of this word, but it belongs only to the holy, who are purified in mind, "who are clean of heart", who are "simple in soul", who are blameless in life, who are free in conscience — theirs it is to hear the discourse concerning this, to them can these mysteries be explained. "For to you it is given", he says, "to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God, but to those", that is, who are not worthy, who are not such as to deserve it nor can be capable of the understanding of secret things, "to those it cannot be given": this priestly…

But let us now see what that soul also does which "hears the voice of one swearing an oath and is a witness", "or" which "sees" something "and is privy to it and does not disclose it", from which it too "has borne his sin" — without doubt his who either did something wickedly or swore. This also, according to the history, builds us up and teaches us never to pollute our consciences in another's sins, nor to lend consent to those who act wickedly. And I call it consent not only to act along with them, but also to keep silent about the things that have been done unlawfully. Do you wish to know that these things agree also with the Gospel precepts? The Lord himself says: "if you see your brother sin, reprove him between yourself and him alone. If he hears you, you have gained your brother. But if he does not hear you, take with you two others or three. But if he does not hear even them,…

It is added in what follows: "and the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: this is the offering of Aaron and of his sons, which they shall offer to the Lord on the day when you shall anoint him, the tenth part of an ephah of fine flour in sacrifice always, half of it in the morning, and half of it after noon. In a pan it shall be made with oil, sprinkled he shall offer it soft, a sacrifice of fragments, a sacrifice for an odor of sweetness to the Lord. The priest who shall be anointed in his stead from among his sons shall make them; an eternal law; all shall be consummated. And every sacrifice of a priest shall be a whole burnt offering, and shall not be eaten." In the other precepts indeed the high priest furnishes his office to the people in offering the sacrifices; but in this commandment he attends to what is proper to himself and carries out what pertains to himself. For he is commanded…

"And every sacrifice which is made in the oven, and everything which is made on the gridiron or in the frying-pan, shall be the priest's who offers it; it shall be his". What do we say? Are we to suppose that almighty God, who gave responses to Moses from heaven, gave precepts about the "oven" and the "gridiron" and the "frying-pan", so that the people might learn through Moses that through these God would become propitious to them, if they fried certain things "in the frying-pan", cooked certain things "in the oven", roasted certain things "on the gridiron"? But "not so" did the children of the Church "learn Christ", nor were they "instructed in him" through the Apostles in such a way, that they should suppose anything so lowly and so cheap concerning "the Lord of majesty". Rather, according to the spiritual sense which the Spirit gives to the Church, let us see what that "sacrifice"…

That our Lord Jesus Christ is called a physician in the divine Scriptures we are fully taught by the sentence of the Lord himself, as he says in the Gospels: "They that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick. For I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." Now every physician compounds medicines beneficial to bodies from the juices of herbs or of trees, or even from the veins of metals or the natures of living creatures. But if someone should chance to look upon these herbs before they are compounded according to the reasoning of the art, then indeed, if they are in the fields or on the mountains, he tramples them underfoot and passes them by as worthless grass. But if he sees them set out in order within a physician's school, though perhaps they give off a bitter and harsh odor, nevertheless he will suspect that they contain something of healing or…

"And the Lord spoke," it says, "unto Moses, saying: Speak unto the children of Israel, and thou shalt say unto them: Whatsoever woman shall have conceived seed and borne a male, she shall be unclean seven days." First let us consider according to the history, whether it does not seem to be added as though superfluously: "the woman who shall have conceived seed and borne a male," as if she could bear a male otherwise than by seed conceived. But it is not added superfluously. For to distinguish her who "conceived and bore" without seed, the lawgiver added this word for the sake of the other women, so that he might designate as "unclean" not every woman who had borne, but her who "had borne with seed conceived." To this may also be added that this law, which is written concerning uncleanness, pertains to women; but concerning Mary it is said that "a virgin" conceived and bore. Let the…

After these things it is written: "keep", it says, "my precepts and do them, I am the Lord", and to these it added: "a man, a man, if he shall have cursed his father or his mother, let him die"; and after many things which it commanded, to which it also appended the penalties of transgression, it adds in the conclusion: "and keep all my precepts and my justifications and my judgments". Whence it seems to me consequent to inquire what is indicated in these single terms. For my part, according to what I have been able to observe, a "precept" or "commandment" is that which, for example, in the decalogue is said: "you shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery"; for this only is enjoined, and the penalty of the deed is not appended. But now indeed the same things are repeated, but with penalties added; for it is said: "a man, a man, whoever shall have committed adultery with the wife of…

But what shall we say concerning the sacrifice of the "ram" bought "at a price" and "at the price of a shekel of the sanctuary", which is commanded to be offered for the expiation of sin? He is going to be rich who can purge his offenses "at the price of a ram". What these riches are, let us seek. The most wise Solomon teaches us, saying: "the redemption of a man's soul is his own proper riches". Do you hear the words of wisdom, how with necessary properties it declares the force of each word? He speaks of riches suited to "the redemption of the soul", and riches not another's nor common, but "proper riches". By which he shows that there are certain "proper riches" and certain riches not proper. But this the Lord more evidently declared in the Gospels, when he says: "but if you have not been faithful in what is another's, who will give you what is your own?", showing that the riches of…

Then the lawgiver adds: "or if he has done any harm to his neighbor, or if he has found something lost." The law of the letter seems to command this, that, if anyone finds what another has lost and it is asked for, he restore it and let it "not perish for him." This too is a useful edification for the hearers. For many think it is without sin if they retain another's property which they have found, and they say: God gave it to me, to whom do I have to render it? Let them learn, therefore, that this sin is like robbery, if anyone does not return what he has found. Yet nevertheless, if the lawgiver had wished only this, which is thought according to the letter, to be understood, he could have said: if he finds what had perished, or what someone had lost. But now, when he says "he has found a perdition," he wished us to understand something more. Those who sin exceedingly are in the…

See, then, how both the "living hen and the cedar wood and the twisted scarlet and the hyssop are dipped in the blood of the young bird and in living water," so that from this, sprinkled and purified from the "water and blood" in which that "hen" too was dipped which is sent forth "into the field," and sprinkled "seven times toward the Lord," he who is being purified may be made clean from all the uncleanness by which he had been possessed from the contagion of leprosy.

But as for what he says: "And Moses brought near the sons of Aaron, and clothed them with tunics and girded them with girdles and put upon them cidaras, as the Lord commanded Moses", it must be attended to what is the difference of the lesser priests to the greater priesthoods. To these neither are double vestments handed over, nor the "ephod", nor the "rational", nor the "ornament of the head", but only the "cidaris" and the "girdles", which bind the tunic. These too, then, receive the grace of the priesthood, and these too discharge the office, but not as that one who is adorned both with the "ephod" and the "rational", who is resplendent "with manifestation and truth", who is decorated with the ornament of the "golden plate". Whence I judge it to be one thing among priests to discharge the office, and another to be instructed in all things and adorned. For anyone can discharge the…

But first of all let us show how these things which are written concerning the sacrifices the Apostle says are "figures" and "forms", whose truth is shown in other things, lest perchance the hearers should think that we presume and violently bend the law of God to another sense than that in which it is written — that is, if no Apostolic authority in these things which we assert should go before. Paul therefore, writing to the Hebrews, namely to those who indeed read the law and had these things meditated upon and well known, but had need of understanding as to how one ought to think concerning the sacrifices, says in this manner: "for Jesus entered not into the holy place made with hands, the copies of the true things, but into heaven itself, that he might now appear before the face of God for us." And again he says of the victims: "for this he did once, by offering himself as a…

With attentive ears and watchful heart hear the consecration of the high priest, or of the priest, because you too, according to the promises of God, are priests of the Lord: "for you are a holy nation and a priesthood." Moses, he says, took according to the command of the Lord "Aaron and his sons", and first indeed he washes them, and afterward he clothes them. Consider more carefully the order of the words: first he washes, afterward he clothes. For you cannot be clothed unless you have first been washed. "Wash yourselves," therefore, "and be clean, and take away your wickednesses from your souls." For unless you have been washed in this manner, you cannot put on the Lord Jesus Christ, according to what the Apostle says: "Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in its lusts." Let Moses, therefore, wash you, let him himself wash you and let him himself clothe…

"And you shall pursue your enemies". What "enemies", except "the devil" himself "and his angels" and the malignant spirits and "the unclean demons"? We shall pursue them not only that we may drive them away from ourselves, but also from others whom they assail, if we keep the divine precepts. "You shall pursue", He says, "your enemies, and they shall fall before you by death". If "God should crush Satan under our feet swiftly", "the enemies shall fall before us by death". By whose "death"? I think, by ours; for if we "mortify our members, which are upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness", if we inflict this death upon our members, "they shall fall before us". How "shall they fall before us"? If you be just, injustice has fallen "before" you; if you be chaste, lust has fallen; if you be pious, impiety has collapsed before you.

And yet: "he shall lay his hand," it says, "upon the head of the victim, and they shall slaughter the calf before the Lord, and the sons of Aaron the priest shall offer the blood, and they shall pour out the blood at the altar round about, which is at the door of the tabernacle of testimony." It can indeed seem to have been said for this reason, that Annas and Caiaphas and the rest were of the sons of Aaron, "all who, taking counsel against Jesus, pronounced him guilty of death" and poured out his blood "around the base of the altar of the tabernacle of testimony." For there the blood is poured out where the altar and its base were, as the Lord himself also said: "because it does not befall a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem." He "placed," then, also "his hand upon the head of the calf," that is, he laid the sins of the human race upon his own body; for he himself is the head of the…

Now, then, let us also inquire into this: what is the cause that a woman, who furnishes a ministry to those being born into this world, is said to be made "unclean" not only when "she has received seed," but also when "she has borne"? Whence also for her purification she is commanded to offer "young pigeons or turtledoves for sin at the door of the tabernacle of testimony," that "the priest may make propitiation for her," as one who owes a propitiation and a purification of sin for the fact that she furnished a ministry to a man being born into this world. For thus it is written: "And the priest shall make propitiation for her, and she shall be cleansed." I dare say nothing in such matters, yet I perceive that certain hidden mysteries are contained in these things, and that there is something of a latent secret, on account of which even "the woman who shall have conceived of seed and…

The Day of Atonement is needed by all who have sinned, and therefore among the solemnities of the law, which contain the figures of the heavenly mysteries, there is held a certain solemnity which is called the Day of Atonement. This, then, which has now been read out, is the legislation of that very solemnity which, as we have said, is called the Day of Atonement. But let us see first what the content of the letter itself intends, so that, while you pray — provided that you so beseech the Lord that you may deserve to be heard — we may be able to receive the grace of the Spirit, through which we may have strength to explain the mysteries which are contained in the law. "Two sons of Aaron died, Nadab and Abihu, when they offered strange fire at the altar of the Lord." It was necessary that Aaron should be instructed by heavenly teaching in what manner he ought to approach the altar, and…

And well is it that the things which are offered from the sacrifice of fine flour are offered "with a full hand, with oil" and "frankincense, for an odor of sweetness to the Lord." This passage the Apostle Paul briefly explained to the Philippians, saying: "I am filled, having received from Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odor of sweetness, a victim accepted, pleasing to God." In which he shows that mercy toward the poor pours oil into the sacrifice of God, but the ministry which is rendered to the saints puts on the sweetness of frankincense. But this is commanded to be done "with a full hand." For thus the same Apostle says, that "he who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly; but he who sows in blessing shall also reap of blessing." There is, however, something in the sacrifice itself which is called the "memorial," which is said to be offered to the Lord. If I…

If, according to the faith of the divine law, these things which are read to us were spoken by the Lord to Moses, I think that, as being the words of God, they ought to be understood not according to the incapacity of the hearers but according to the majesty of the one speaking. "The Lord," it says, "spoke." What is "the Lord"? Let the Apostle answer you, and learn from him that "the Lord is spirit." But if the word of the Apostle does not suffice for you, hear the Lord himself saying in the Gospels that "God is spirit." If therefore both the Lord and God is "spirit," the things which the spirit speaks we ought to hear spiritually. But I say yet something more: that the things the Lord speaks are to be believed not only spiritual, but even spirit. This I will prove not by my own opinion, but from the Gospels; hear our Lord and Savior saying to his disciples: "the words which I have…

Let us therefore now see what is the "deposit" which each of the faithful has received. I think that we have received both our own soul and our body as a deposit from God. And do you wish to see another, greater "deposit" which you have received from God? To your very soul God entrusted "his own image and likeness." This deposit, therefore, must be restored by you as whole as it is established to have been received by you. For if you are merciful, "as your Father in heaven is merciful," the image of God is in you and you preserve the "deposit" whole. If you are perfect, "as your Father also in heaven is perfect," the deposit of the image of God remains in you. And likewise all the rest: if you are devout, if you are just, if holy, if "pure in heart," and if all the things which are present in God by nature subsist in you by imitation, the "deposit" of the divine image is safe with you.…

Let us now see what also is to be understood by "partnership." Do you suppose there is anyone who ought to be admonished according to the letter, lest perchance in a matter of money, or in any other kind of partnership, he deceive his partner by fraud? Of the utmost misery is that soul into which this kind of fraud can still fall. Yet nevertheless, because there is much fragility in man, let us admonish concerning these things also, since not even the Apostle was reluctant to command them. For he says: "let no one overreach his brother in business, since God is the avenger of all these things." But now let us inquire what also is the "partnership of the spirit." Hear the Apostle speaking concerning these very things: "if there is any comfort of love, if any partnership of the spirit, if any bowels of compassion, fulfill my joy." You see how the Apostle Paul understood the law of…

Everyone who is a priest among men is small and slight in comparison with that priest of whom God said: "you are a priest forever after the order of Melchizedek". But he is the "great priest" who is able "to penetrate the heavens" and to pass beyond the whole of creation and to ascend to him who "dwells in light inaccessible", the God and Father of the universe. For this reason the one too who among the Jews was called the "great priest" did indeed enter into the holy places, but ones made by hand, built of stones; he did not ascend into heaven nor was he able to stand before the "Father of lights". But because he was fulfilling the shadow and image of these things, therefore also he bore the name of "great priest" by way of shadow and image.
